summary.text: Amber is tree resin that has become a fossil, prized for its orange to brown color and worked as a gemstone since ancient times.
Because it starts out as soft, sticky resin, amber sometimes holds bits of animals and plants trapped inside it.
Its ancient Greek name, elektron, gave us the word electricity, because amber can carry a charge of static electricity.

facts.label: Known varieties
facts.value: Over 150 types in five chemical classes

facts.label: Ancient trade route
facts.value: The Amber Road, linking the Baltic and Mediterranean

items.prompt: A fly sits perfectly preserved inside a piece of amber. How did it most likely end up there?

options.label: It crawled into a crack in hard stone
It got stuck in sticky resin that later fossilized
It was frozen in ice that later turned to stone
It was washed into a mineral-rich spring

items.explain: Amber begins as soft, sticky tree resin, so small creatures and plant bits can get caught in it before it fossilizes.

items.prompt: The Greek word for amber, elektron, is the root of the word "electric". What property of amber explains the link?

options.label: It glows faintly when warmed up
It forms in trees struck by lightning
It carries current as well as metal
It can hold a charge of static

items.explain: Amber can bear a static charge because it is a good insulator, which is why elektron led to words like electric.

items.prompt: You drop a chunk of amber into a glass of fresh water, then into a glass of very salty water. What happens?

options.label: It sinks in the fresh water but floats in the salty water
It floats in both glasses of water
It sinks to the bottom in both glasses
It floats in the fresh water but sinks in the salty water

items.explain: Amber is denser than water, so it sinks in fresh water, yet it floats in strongly salty water.

items.prompt: A hobbyist heats a lump of amber above 200 °C. What happens to it?

options.label: It softens back into sticky resin
It hardens into clear glass
It breaks down into oil and black residue
It crumbles into a fine white powder

items.explain: Above 200 °C amber decomposes, giving off an oil and leaving a black residue called amber pitch.

items.prompt: A piece of amber is cloudy all the way through instead of clear. What can cause this?

options.label: Water slowly soaked into it
Huge numbers of tiny bubbles inside it
It froze while it was still soft
Sunlight bleached away its color

items.explain: So-called bony amber gets its cloudy look from countless tiny bubbles in the resin.

items.prompt: Researchers want to see what is trapped inside a dark, opaque lump of amber without cutting it. What can they use?

options.label: A strong ultraviolet lamp
A powerful magnifying glass
A bath of very salty water
High-energy, high-detail X-rays

items.explain: Even in dark or opaque amber, trapped inclusions can be imaged with high-energy, high-contrast, high-resolution X-rays.
